explain.key: Casey describes a hyperthreaded core as running only one of its states "at a given time" and switching quickly. That's a fair first picture, and he says there's "tons more to talk about". On modern chips, instructions from both hardware threads are usually in flight in the same core at the same time, sharing its execution units. When one thread stalls (for example, waiting on memory), the other keeps those units busy. That's why a hyperthread doesn't count as a whole extra core: two threads on one core usually finish somewhat faster than one, but nowhere near twice as fast.
